This young Arab commander, serving the Umayyad Caliphate, captured the region of Sindh around 712, marking the start of Muslim rule in South Asia — who is he?
Muhammad ibn al-Qasim: Umayyad general and governor of Sindh (695–715)

Claiming to be the successor to the Holy Roman Empire and the 1871–1918 German Empire, this 'Third Reich' was meant to last a thousand years but collapsed after just 12 when Berlin fell in 1945. What was it?
Nazi Germany: German state from 1933 to 1945.

A Shia dissident who fled a death sentence and spent 24 years in exile coordinating anti-Saddam guerrillas, this leader of the Islamic Dawa Party went on to serve as Iraq's prime minister from 2006 to 2014 — who is he?
Nouri al-Maliki: Prime Minister of Iraq from 2006 to 2014. Three years after the 2003 invasion of Iraq, al-Maliki became the country's first post-Saddam full-term prime minister.

The eldest son of Henry the Fowler, this 10th-century king unified the German tribes and became Holy Roman Emperor in 962 after installing family members in the realm's most powerful duchies — who was he?
Otto the Great: Holy Roman Emperor from 962 to 973.
Hailed by the historian Thucydides as 'the first citizen of Athens,' this statesman transformed the Delian League into an Athenian empire during the city's Golden Age — who is he?
In the Book of Genesis, this unnamed woman falsely accused Joseph of assault after he spurned her advances, landing him in prison — later Islamic tradition names her Zuleikha. Who is she?
Potiphar's wife: Figure from Jewish and Muslim tradition.
An Indian politician born in 1970, this member of the Indian National Congress serves as the 12th leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha and represents Rae Bareli. Who is he?
Rahul Gandhi: 12th Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha since 2024.
He made his film debut as the boozy title character in a 1987 comedy, then decades later earned an Oscar nomination for playing Jack Hock in Can You Ever Forgive Me? — who is he?
Born in Newcastle upon Tyne to Russian émigré parents, this KGB spy ring leader in New York was arrested by the FBI on espionage charges in 1957 — who was he?
Prince Gustaf Adolf, Duke of Västerbotten
In October 2025, she became the first woman ever to serve as Prime Minister of Japan — who is she?
Sanae Takaichi: Prime Minister of Japan since 2025. Takaichi's administration has consistently polled high in approval ratings.

Entering a power-sharing arrangement with his father in 2022, this politician became president after winning 73% of the vote in what's widely considered a sham election, making his nation the first in modern Central Asia ruled by a father-son dynasty — who is he?
Serdar Berdimuhamedow: President of Turkmenistan since 2022.

In 1793, Royalist rebels in this vital French naval port — home to a third of the French fleet — invited a 13,000-strong Anglo-Spanish force to help hold the city against advancing Republican troops — what military engagement was this?
Siege of Toulon (1793): Part of the War of the First Coalition.

This doctrine holding that governing authority is legitimate to some degree — especially over taxation and production — gained traction in American political discourse during the 1930s and '40s, its opposite being anarchism — what's it called?

Statism: Doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree. In political science, statism or etatism (from French, état 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.

Founder of a political party built around reforming Japan's public broadcaster, this activist-turned-politician won a House of Councillors seat in 2019 before forfeiting it to run in a by-election — who is he?
Born into Virginia's planter class, he served as second vice president before becoming the third U.S. president — and famously penned the Declaration of Independence — who was he?
Thomas Jefferson: Founding Father, U.S. president from 1801 to 1809.
As chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority, this Royal Court adviser also owned Spanish club Almería from 2019 to 2025 — who is he?
A free-love advocate and women's rights activist, she ran for president of the United States in 1872 — widely cited as the first woman to do so; who was she?
Victoria Woodhull: American women's suffrage activist (1838–1927)
Sparked by a dispute over Maria Theresa's right to inherit the Habsburg throne, this 1740–1748 conflict began when Prussia seized the wealthy province of Silesia — what was this conflict called?
War of the Austrian Succession: 1740–1748 war between European powers.

Known as the 'Mother of the Nation,' this South African anti-apartheid activist and politician served in parliament and led the ANC Women's League after marrying the country's future president in 1958 — who is she?
Winnie Mandela: South African activist and politician (1936–2018)

After helping secure the Qing dynasty's abdication, this Chinese general became the Republic's first formal president, only to declare himself emperor in 1915 and abdicate again months later — who was he?
Yuan Shikai: First president of the Republic of China (1859–1916)
Which one below was born first?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (born 1906) is the earliest of the four. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Franz Reichelt (born 1878) is the earliest of the four. The parachute failed to deploy and he plummeted 57 metres (187 ft) to his death.
Which of these four began earliest?
Messerschmitt Bf 109 (founded 1937) is the earliest of the four.
Perl (founded 1987) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Horace Bénédict de Saussure is a physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
Dolph Lundgren is a chemist. Hans "Dolph" Lundgren (Swedish: [ˈdɔlːf ˈlɵ̌nːdɡreːn]; born 3 November 1957) is a Swedish-American actor, filmmaker, and martial artist.
What is the atomic number of Unbiquadium?
Unbiquadium, also known as element 124 or eka-uranium, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has placeholder symbol Ubq and atomic number 124.
In what year was Gabor Maté born?
Gabor Maté ( GAH-bor MAH-tay; born January 1944) is a Canadian physician and author.
In what year was Linus Torvalds born?
Linus Torvalds: Linus Benedict Torvalds (born 28 December 1969) is a Finnish and American software engineer who is the creator and lead developer of the Linux kernel since 1991.
In what year was John Money born?
John Money: Money researched paraphilia, including pedophilia, and pioneered the use of drug treatment to extinguish the libido of sex offenders.
In what year did Luke the Evangelist die?
Luke the Evangelist was one of the Four Evangelists—the four traditionally ascribed authors of the canonical gospels.
In what year did Charles Babbage die?
Charles Babbage (26 December 1791 – 18 October 1871) was an English polymath.
In what year was Glutathione discovered?
Glutathione (GSH,) is a tripeptide made of the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.
In what year was Morphine discovered?
Morphine, formerly known as morphium, is an opiate found naturally in opium, a dark brown resin produced by drying the latex of opium poppies (Papaver somniferum).
Acetylcysteine: Pfizer. It has been used to treat lactobezoar in infants.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-35 from?
Sukhoi Su-35: Soviet Union. The type was originally developed by the Soviet Union from the Su-27 and was known as the Su-27M.
Who is credited with discovering Palladium?
Palladium: William Hyde Wollaston. Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
Who is credited with discovering Pectin?
Pectin: Henri Braconnot. The principal chemical component of pectin is galacturonic acid (a sugar acid derived from galactose).
Who is credited with discovering Oxygen?
Oxygen: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
The simplest alkyne, this colorless gas owes its straight-line shape to a carbon-carbon triple bond — and though pure it's odorless, commercial grades reek thanks to impurities. What is it?
Acetylene (systematic name: ethyne) is a chemical compound with the formula C2H2 and structure HCCH.

Native to South America but cultivated in Europe since the 17th century for its fragrant oil, this flowering member of the verbena family is better known by a common name referencing a citrus fruit — what's its scientific name?
Aloysia citrodora is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family Verbenaceae, native to South America.
Best known for his laws of planetary motion, this German astronomer has also been called the 'father of science fiction' for his novel Somnium. Who is he?

Antelope is any of the extant or recently extinct species of the ruminant artiodactyl family Bovidae, which are indigenous to most of Africa, India, the Middle East, Central Asia, and a small area of Russia.
Doctors reach for this NSAID not just for aches but to treat Kawasaki disease and rheumatic fever — and it's famous for its blood-thinning effect on platelets. What is it?
Aspirin is the genericized trademark for acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation, and as an antithrombotic.

Found naturally in many plants and abbreviated "Bz," this white crystalline compound is the simplest of the aromatic carboxylic acids and lends its salts to the world of food preservatives — what is it?
Benzoic acid is a white or colorless crystalline organic compound with the formula C6H5COOH, whose structure consists of a benzene ring (C6H6) with a carboxyl (C(=O)OH) substituent.
With the formula B(OH)3 and found in nature as the mineral sassolite, this weak, water-soluble compound of boron serves as an antiseptic, insecticide, and flame retardant — which acid?
Boric acid is a compound of boron, oxygen, and hydrogen with formula B(OH)3.

Native to the Philippines and nearby Southeast Asia, this small sour citrus fruit — a natural hybrid of kumquat and mandarin — flavors everything from marinades to beverages in Filipino cooking — which fruit?
Calamansi (Citrus microcarpa), also known as calamondin, Philippine lime, or Philippine lemon, is a citrus hybrid cultivated predominantly in the Philippines.
Separated from the small intestine by the ileocecal valve, this pouch — whose Latin root means 'blind' — kicks off the large intestine and, in herbivores, helps ferment cellulose. What is it?
Cecum (plural ceca or) is a pouch within the peritoneum that is considered to be the beginning of the large intestine.
This roughly 24-hour internal biological cycle, generated within an organism but tuned by cues like daylight, is regulated by an internal biological clock — what is it called?
Circadian rhythm is a natural oscillation that repeats roughly every 24 hours.
Entering service with Strategic Air Command in 1960, this four-engine, delta-wing supersonic bomber was the first in the world capable of Mach 2 — name the aircraft?

Convair B-58 Hustler is a supersonic strategic bomber, the first capable of Mach 2 flight. To achieve the high speeds desired, Convair chose a delta wing design used by contemporary interceptors such as the Convair F-102.
Nearly every genus in this taxonomic family of armadillos is extinct, except for one genus that still includes eight living species today. Name the family?
Dasypodidae is a family of mostly extinct genera of armadillos.
Found in nighttime cold remedies like NyQuil and paired with vitamin B6 for pregnancy-related nausea, this antihistamine is an inverse agonist at the H1 receptor — which drug?
Doxylamine is an antihistamine medication used to treat insomnia and allergies, and - in combination with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) - to treat morning sickness in pregnant women.
The tallest native bird in Australia and the third-tallest living bird overall, this flightless ratite can grow up to 1.9 metres tall. What bird is it?
Emu (Dromaius novaehollandiae) is a species of flightless bird endemic to Australia, where it is the tallest native bird.
Known for thin, tapered wings built for high-speed flight and rapid turns, this genus of roughly 40 raptor species includes types called hobbies and kestrels — what are they?
Falcon are birds of prey in the genus Falco, which includes about 40 species.
This West Point graduate, eighth in his class of 670, commanded Apollo 8's historic flight around the Moon in 1968 — who is he?
Frank Borman (March 14, 1928 - November 7, 2023) was an American United States Air Force (USAF) colonel, aeronautical engineer, NASA astronaut, test pilot, and businessman.
The most aggressive and common cancer to originate in the brain, this tumor is thought to arise from cells called astrocytes and carries a grim prognosis — what is it?
Glioblastoma (GBM), is the most aggressive and most common type of cancer that originates in the brain, and has a very poor prognosis for survival.
Prehensile and multi-fingered, this appendage sits at the end of primates' forearms, though a few other animals like koalas and raccoons are sometimes described as having one too — which body part?
Hand is a prehensile, multi-fingered appendage located at the end of the forearm or forelimb of primates such as humans, chimpanzees, monkeys, and lemurs.
Originally a variable measure equal to one-twelfth of the night or day in the ancient Near East, this unit of time is now fixed at exactly 3,600 seconds — name this unit?
Hour (symbol: h; also abbreviated hr) is a unit of time historically reckoned as 124 of a day and defined contemporarily as exactly 3,600 seconds.
This contagious bacterial skin infection most often shows up as yellowish crusts on a child's face, arms, or legs, and spreads easily in crowded day cares and contact sports — what is it?
Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection that involves the superficial skin.
This French mathematician of algebraic topology and number theory pulled off a rare double: the Fields Medal in 1954 and, nearly fifty years later, the very first Abel Prize. Who was he?
Jean-Pierre Serre (born 15 September 1926) is a French mathematician who has made contributions to algebraic topology, algebraic geometry and algebraic number theory.
This pain-relieving, fever-reducing drug belongs to the propionic acid class of anti-inflammatories and hit the market in 1980, thirteen years after being patented — what is it?
Ketoprofen is one of the propionic acid class of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) with analgesic and antipyretic effects.
Distinguished from its cousins the pikas by short furry tails and elongated ears and hind legs, this mammal family comprises over 70 species we commonly call rabbits and hares — which family?
Leporidae is the family of rabbits and hares (Lepus), containing over 70 species of extant mammals in all.
Serving under Chancellor Adenauer, this economist championed West Germany's postwar economic miracle before becoming chancellor himself in 1963 — who is he?
Ludwig Erhard (4 February 1897 - 5 May 1977) was a German politician and economist who served as the second chancellor of West Germany from 1963 until 1966.
Covering everything from B2B deals to a government's 'Got Milk?'-style campaigns, this business pillar means acquiring, satisfying and retaining customers — what is this discipline called?
Marketing is the act of acquiring, satisfying and retaining customers. It is one of the primary components of business management and commerce.
Connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum to the pons, this brainstem structure plays a role in vision, hearing, and staying alert -- what is it called?
Midbrain is the uppermost portion of the brainstem connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum with the pons.
This semiaquatic rodent can stay submerged for up to seventeen minutes, propelled mainly by its webbed hind feet while its long, scaly tail helps steer — what animal is it?
Muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) is a medium-sized semiaquatic rodent.
First isolated by Scottish physician Daniel Rutherford, which group-15 nonmetal with atomic number 7 is the most abundant species in Earth's atmosphere?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known for causing bones that fracture easily, this group of genetic disorders can also produce blue-tinted eye whites, short stature, and hearing loss. Name the condition?
Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), colloquially known as brittle bone disease, is a group of genetic disorders that all result in bones that break easily.
Sometimes mistaken for wild pigs, these New World ungulates roam from the southwestern U.S. through Central and South America and into Trinidad — name the family?
Peccary (also javelinas or skunk pigs) are pig-like ungulates of the family Tayassuidae (New World pigs).

This subdiscipline of biology examines how organisms, organs, cells, and biomolecules carry out their chemical and physical functions, and its name derives from Greek words for 'nature' and 'study of' — what is it?
Physiology (from Ancient Greek (phsis) 'nature, origin' and - (-loga) 'study of') is the scientific study of functions and mechanisms in a living system.
A colorless salt that looks deceptively like sugar and dissolves easily in water, this compound is mostly used in gold mining — but a 200-to-300-milligram dose will kill nearly any human. What is it?
Potassium cyanide is a compound with the formula KCN.

Found across Africa, Asia, and Australia, this family of nonvenomous snakes includes some of the world's largest and kills by coiling to suffocate rather than by injecting venom — what is the family called?

Pythonidae are a family of nonvenomous snakes found in Africa, Asia, and Australia. The taxonomy of pythons has evolved, and they are now known to be more closely related to sunbeam snakes and the Mexican burrowing python.

A brilliant English anatomist who coined the word 'Dinosauria,' meaning roughly 'terrible reptile,' he accepted that evolution happened but was an outspoken critic of Darwin's account of it. Who was he?
Richard Owen (20 July 1804 - 18 December 1892) was an English biologist, comparative anatomist and palaeontologist.
Nicknamed the seven-year itch, this contagious skin condition is caused by a microscopic burrowing mite and thrives in crowded places like prisons and care homes — what is it?
Scabies (also sometimes known as the seven-year itch) is a contagious human skin infestation by the tiny (0.2-0.45 mm) mite Sarcoptes scabiei, variety hominis.

Built for the Marine Corps by adding a third engine and a seventh main rotor blade to an earlier heavy-lift helicopter, this aircraft entered service in 1981 and flies from Navy ships — which helicopter?
Sikorsky CH-53E Super Stallion is a heavy lift helicopter operated by the United States military.
Doctors examine the color of this coughed-up airway mucus — greenish or yellow tints can hint at infection, though not which organism caused it — what is it?
Sputum is mucus that is coughed up from the lower airways (the trachea and bronchi).

Caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously announces itself with a single painless ulcer called a chancre, then a rash that loves the palms and soles — which sexually transmitted disease is it?

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum. The signs and symptoms depend on the stage it presents: primary, secondary, latent or tertiary.

Beloved by biologists for its wild morphological variation and elaborate nest-building, this northern fish tolerates big swings in salinity, living in the sea but breeding in fresh water — what is it?
Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) is a fish native to most inland and coastal waters north of 30N.

It spawned a maritime patrol version (the Tu-142) and even a passenger airliner (the Tu-114), and Russia expects to keep flying this propeller-driven bomber until at least 2040 — which aircraft is it?
Tupolev Tu-95 (NATO reporting name: "Bear") is a Soviet nuclear-capable large, four-engine turboprop strategic bomber and missile platform.

Belonging to the same family as kangaroos, this informally named group of smaller macropods is native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations as far away as Hawaii and the UK — what are they called?
Wallaby is a small or middle-sized macropod native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations in New Zealand, Hawaii, the United Kingdom and other countries.
Also called humped cattle for the fatty growth on its shoulders, this South Asian breed group is used for everything from plowing to dairy, and even kept as pets in miniature form — what is it?
Zebu (Bos indicus), also known as indicine cattle and humped cattle, is a species or subspecies of domestic cattle originating in South Asia.

Typically affecting women between 35 and 50, this uterine condition occurs when endometrial-like tissue grows within the muscular wall of the uterus, causing painful, heavy periods — what is it called?
Adenomyosis: Extension of endometrial tissue into the myometrium.
On 18 March 1965, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first person to walk in space, spending over twelve minutes outside his capsule during a Voskhod mission — who is he?

Capable of constantly changing its shape by extending and retracting temporary 'false feet,' this single-celled organism turns up across nearly every branch of the eukaryotic tree of life — what is it?
Shed and regrown every year on most male deer, this bony head growth serves as both a weapon and a symbol of sexual attraction — what is it?
Antler: Skull projections found in deer.
Dubbed the 'Prophet of the Space Age,' this English science fiction author co-wrote the screenplay for 2001: A Space Odyssey and formed sci-fi's 'Big Three' with Heinlein and Asimov — who is he?
Arthur C. Clarke: British science fiction writer (1917–2008)
With six species native to Africa (and one also found in Arabia), these large Old World monkeys have dog-like muzzles and have existed for at least two million years — what are they called?

This Swiss-American engineer was the only one of a famous physicist's three known biological grandsons to survive childhood, and later earned patents in electronics while working at Texas Instruments — who was he?
The only trijet ever produced by its manufacturer, this airliner entered service with Eastern Air Lines in 1964 powered by three rear-mounted turbofans?
Ranging from roughly seawater-strength up to a fully saturated 26%, which salty solution is used for pickling food, de-icing roads, and turns up as a wastewater byproduct of desalination?
Brine: Concentrated solution of salt in water.
Named for the Latin word for the first day of the month, this daisy-family genus is commonly called marigold and is prized in herbal and cosmetic products — which plant?
Calendula: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Its Greek-derived genus name Xylocopa literally means 'wood-cutter,' fitting for an insect that burrows nesting tunnels into dead wood or bamboo — which insect is it?
Carpenter bee: Common name for a genus of bees.

Serving as royal executioner under Louis XVI and later chief executioner of the First Republic, this Frenchman carried out nearly 3,000 executions during his 40-year career, including those of the king, queen, and Robespierre — who is he?

Also bearing the names Krebs and TCA, this loop of biochemical reactions unlocks the energy in nutrients via the oxidation of acetyl-CoA — and is thought to be one of the earliest metabolic components. What is it?
Citric acid cycle: Interconnected biochemical reactions releasing energy.
In this prolonged state of deep unconsciousness, a person cannot be awakened, shows no normal sleep-wake cycle, and may even be induced deliberately during general anesthesia — what is it?
Coma: State of unconsciousness. The person may experience respiratory and circulatory problems due to the body's inability to maintain normal bodily functions.
First described in 1880 by a French neurologist, this rare delusion convinces sufferers that they are dead, don't exist, or have lost their internal organs — what is it called?
Cotard's syndrome: Delusion that one is dead or non-existent.
Bred in Germany with short legs and a long body to chase badgers into their burrows, which hound breed comes in smooth-, wire-, and long-haired varieties?
Sold as Voltaren and taken by mouth, suppository, injection, skin gel, or even eye drops, this NSAID eases pain and inflammation like gout for up to eight hours a dose — what is it?
Revered by Ancient Egyptians as the god Khepri for rolling the sun across the sky, which insect feeds exclusively on feces?
Dung beetle: Informal group of insects.
This genus of deciduous trees, once popular as ornamental street trees across Europe and North America, was decimated by a fungal disease spread by bark beetles — which tree?
Elm: Flowering, deciduous trees, family Ulmaceae.

Defined by a single oxygen atom bridging two organyl groups (R−O−R′), this class of organic compounds includes a once-standard surgical anesthetic that lends its common one-word name to the whole family. What class of compound is this?
Ether: Organic compounds made of alkyl/aryl groups bound to oxygen (R–O–R')
Known for its smooth silvery-grey bark and toxin-laced but edible nuts, this deciduous tree native to Europe includes the striking copper-leaved cultivar among its ornamentals — which species?
Fagus sylvatica: Species of deciduous tree. It is native to much of Europe, growing in humid climates.
This normal, occasionally embarrassing bodily process brings intestinal gas to the rectum, pressurizes it with muscle contractions, and releases it through the anus — what is it?
Flatulence: Bodily function of expelling intestinal gas from the anus.
Known as the brain's chief inhibitory neurotransmitter, this compound is also sold as a dietary supplement despite debate over whether it crosses the blood-brain barrier — what is it?
GABA: Main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain.
Endemic to China and sporting a handy 'thumb' on its forepaw to grip bamboo, this black-and-white bear weighs in around 100 to 115 kg — what animal is it?
Giant panda: Species of bear. The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), also known as the panda bear or simply panda, is a bear species endemic to China.
Sporting pied black-and-white plumage with a red patch on its lower belly, this Palearctic bird drums on trees to mark territory and excavate nest holes — which species?
Great spotted woodpecker: Species of bird. The great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major) is a medium-sized woodpecker with pied black and white plumage and a red patch on the lower belly.
Caused by mutations in the ABCA12 gene, this severe genetic skin disorder covers newborns in thick, cracked plates resembling armor — what is it?
Harlequin-type ichthyosis: Genetic skin disease. Harlequin-type ichthyosis is a genetic disorder that results in thickened skin over nearly the entire body at birth.

Bred by Polynesians in the pre-Columbian era from two Pacific island species, this tropical flowering plant is the national flower of Malaysia and the unofficial national flower of Haiti — what is it?
Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis: Hybrid species of flowering plant. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant in the tropics and subtropics.
Carl Wilhelm Scheele pinned down this gas's composition in 1777; it's flammable, smells of rotten eggs, and kills by blocking cellular respiration much like cyanide — what colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen sulfide: Poisonous and flammable gas. Hydrogen sulfide (preferred IUPAC name and American English) or hydrogen sulphide (Commonwealth English) is a chemical compound with the formula H2S.

Named for the indigo-blue line seen in its spectrum when discovered in 1863, this soft, silvery-white metal with atomic number 49 is used to make the transparent conductive coating on flat-panel displays — what is it?
Indium: Chemical element with atomic number 49 (In)
An English mathematician who shaped matrix and invariant theory, he founded the American Journal of Mathematics while leading the field at Johns Hopkins — who was he?
Hailed as a 'miracle worker' in 1955, this researcher refused to patent his polio vaccine so it could spread worldwide for free — who is he?
Jonas Salk: American inventor of the polio vaccine (1914–1995)
A German mechanical engineer turned economist, he founded a famous annual gathering of global leaders in 1971 and chaired it until stepping down in 2025. Who is he?
Klaus Schwab: Founder of the World Economic Forum (born 1938)
A hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange, this small evergreen tree may have first appeared in northeastern India, and its fruit's juice is about 5–6% citric acid — what is it?

This anatomic form of lung infection causes inflammatory fluid to consolidate across an entire continuous section of one lung, and in children shows up instead as a rounded pattern due to immature air-pore connections — what is it?
Lobar pneumonia: Lung infection. It is one of three anatomic classifications of pneumonia (the other being bronchopneumonia and atypical pneumonia).
A field of artificial intelligence built on statistics and optimization, it develops algorithms that learn from data and handle unseen examples without being explicitly programmed — what is it?
Machine learning: Subset of artificial intelligence. Statistics and mathematical optimisation methods compose the foundations of machine learning.
On April 3, 1973, this Motorola engineer made history's first public call from a handheld cell phone on a Manhattan sidewalk — who is he?
Cataloged as a nebula by a French astronomer in 1781, this supergiant elliptical galaxy boasts roughly 15,000 globular clusters, a hundred times more than our own — which galaxy is it?
Messier 87: Galaxy in the constellation Virgo.

This Serbian polymath — mathematician, astronomer, civil engineer — explained Earth's long-term climate swings by tracking our planet's shifting position relative to the Sun, a theory of cycles that now bears his name. Who was he?
Milutin Milanković: Serbian scientist and professor (1879–1958)
This Bangladeshi economist founded Grameen Bank and pioneered modern microcredit, winning the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize before later leading an interim government — who is he?
Muhammad Yunus: Bangladeshi economist and statesman (born 1940)
Carried harmlessly in the noses of about 10% of adults, this bacterium is the only cause of bacterial meningitis known to occur in epidemics, especially across Africa and Asia — which microbe?
Neisseria meningitidis: Species of bacterium that can cause meningitis.
A subsonic flying wing with a crew of two to three, this nuclear-capable stealth aircraft was built to slip past sophisticated air defenses for the US Air Force — what is it?
Northrop B-2 Spirit: American heavy strategic bomber.

Sitting between tissue and a full body system in life's hierarchy, this general term describes a structural unit built from functional tissue (parenchyma) plus supportive tissue (stroma), as seen in the intestinal wall — what is such a unit called?
Organ (biology): Collection of tissues with similar functions.
This skin sensation includes the classic 'pins and needles' feeling when a limb falls asleep, and can also be triggered by hitting your funny bone — what is it called?
Paresthesia: Dermal sensation with no physical cause.
Created by Larry Wall in 1987 as a Unix scripting tool for report processing, this language's planned sixth version was eventually spun off and renamed Raku — which programming language?
Perl: Interpreted programming language first released in 1987.
This Dutch experimental physicist shared the 1902 Nobel Prize with Hendrik Lorentz for discovering and explaining an effect that now bears his name — who was he?
Covered in sharp keratin quills for defense, this rodent's largest species ranks as the third-biggest living rodent in the world, behind only the capybara and the beaver. What animal is it?
Porcupine: Rodent with a coat of sharp spines.
Nicknamed 'gold cap' and 'golden halo,' this is the world's best-known psilocybin-containing mushroom thanks to its wide distribution and how easily it's cultivated — which species?
Psilocybe cubensis: Species of fungus. It belongs to the fungus family Hymenogastraceae and was previously known as Stropharia cubensis.
Also known as steelhead in its sea-run form, this North American Pacific species shows off a vivid reddish stripe along its flank in breeding males — which fish?
Rainbow trout: Fresh-water species of fish.
Made of a large and small subunit built from RNA and protein, which cellular structure translates messenger RNA into chains of amino acids?
Ribosome: Macromolecular machine that synthesizes proteins in cells.

Built by a Swedish manufacturer, this single-engine fighter was the first mass-produced canard-design aircraft and the first with a digital avionics computer, unsurpassed until the Tornado arrived in 1981 — which jet?
Saab 37 Viggen: 1967 Swedish fighter aircraft family.
Native to cold-temperate Eurasia, this spiny deciduous shrub yields a fruit and oil prized in both cooking and cosmetics — what plant is it?
Sea buckthorn: Species of flowering plant in the family Elaeagnaceae.
